summary: Moves TCP NewReno's Fast Retransmit and Fast Recovery algorithms from RFC 2582 to the standards track, specifying the Careful variant, which avoids unnecessary repeated fast retransmits after a timeout. It obsoletes RFC 2582 and was replaced by RFC 6582.

plainLanguage.summary: When some packets get lost, TCP must recover without panicking. NewReno is a way to fix several losses in a row without slowing too much.

questions: how does newreno handle multiple packet losses
why is newreno better than reno
subtitle: An improvement to TCP's recovery when multiple packets are lost in a single window of data.

tldr.problem: When TCP loses multiple packets from a single transmission window without SACK (Selective Acknowledgment), the standard Reno algorithm performs poorly because it can only infer one packet loss at a time from the acknowledgment sequence.
tldr.mechanism: NewReno adds a 'recover' variable to track what was outstanding when loss was detected, and responds to partial acknowledgments by inferring and retransmitting the next unacknowledged segment. This allows recovery from multiple losses without waiting for retransmission timeouts.
tldr.outcome: NewReno became widely deployed as the standard fast recovery algorithm for non-SACK TCP. RFC 3782 advances the Careful variant to Standards Track status, replacing RFC 2582 and becoming obsoleted by RFC 6582.

today: RFC 3782 established NewReno as the Standards Track algorithm for TCP fast recovery without SACK. It is now obsoleted by RFC 6582, which consolidated subsequent clarifications. NewReno remains widely deployed in TCP stacks for non-SACK scenarios, while SACK-capable implementations use more sophisticated loss recovery algorithms. Modern implementations increasingly support SACK or even QUIC, but NewReno remains important for broad compatibility.

sections.title: The Problem: Multiple Packet Losses
sections.content:
TCP's Reno Fast Retransmit and Fast Recovery algorithms (RFC 2581) work well when only one packet is lost from a transmission window. When the sender sees three duplicate acknowledgments, it infers a packet loss and retransmits the lost packet. However, if multiple packets are lost from the same window of data, Reno's algorithm breaks down.

Without SACK (Selective Acknowledgment), TCP has limited information. When it receives acknowledgments from the receiver, it can only see the highest contiguous sequence number acknowledged, not which individual packets arrived. If packets 5, 6, and 7 are lost from a window, the receiver will acknowledge up to packet 4 repeatedly. Reno Fast Retransmit will retransmit packet 5, but then the next useful information arrives only when the receiver acknowledges past packet 5, which might take a long time if the network is lossy. This means Reno can retransmit at most one packet per window of lost packets, leading to poor performance when several packets are dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: Regular TCP can figure out when one package is lost by counting duplicate replies. But if several packages are lost, it can't tell which ones, so it has to keep guessing and resending very slowly.

sections.title: The NewReno Algorithm: Six Steps
sections.content:
NewReno improves on Reno by introducing a 'recover' variable that tracks the highest sequence number sent when loss was detected. When three duplicate ACKs arrive, the sender first checks whether the cumulative acknowledgment field covers more data than 'recover'. If yes, Fast Retransmit is entered (step 1A), the congestion window is reduced, and 'recover' is updated to the current highest sent sequence number. If no, the duplicate ACKs are ignored (step 1B), treating them as noise rather than a real loss.

In step 5, the critical difference appears: when an ACK arrives, the sender checks if it acknowledges all data up to 'recover'. If yes, Fast Recovery ends (full acknowledgment). If no (partial acknowledgment), the sender infers that the next unacknowledged segment is lost, retransmits it, deflates the congestion window by the amount newly acknowledged, and stays in Fast Recovery to handle further packet losses. This approach allows recovery from multiple losses without waiting for a retransmission timeout.
sections.plainLanguage: NewReno remembers what packet numbers were being sent when loss started. Then it watches the acknowledgments carefully: if the sender gets a partial acknowledgment (meaning some packets got through but not all), it assumes the next missing packet is lost and resends it. This way it can figure out and resend all the missing packets quickly.

sections.title: Partial Acknowledgments and Window Deflation
sections.content:
The key insight of NewReno is handling partial acknowledgments during Fast Recovery. A partial ACK acknowledges some new data but not all the data that was outstanding when loss was detected. When this happens, NewReno (step 5):

  • Retransmits the first unacknowledged segment, inferring it was lost
  • Deflates the congestion window (cwnd) by subtracting the amount of new data acknowledged
  • Adds back one SMSS (Sender Maximum Segment Size) if the partial ACK acknowledged at least one SMSS of new data
  • Sends a new segment if the congestion window permits
  • Resets the retransmit timer (only on the first partial ACK)

This partial window deflation ensures that approximately ssthresh (slow-start threshold) amount of data remains outstanding, allowing steady recovery without oscillation. The sender stays in Fast Recovery after each partial ACK, retransmitting one additional packet per round-trip time until all losses are recovered.
sections.plainLanguage: Each time a partial acknowledgment arrives, NewReno does three things: resends the next missing packet, shrinks the sending window a bit (but adds one packet back), and if allowed, sends a new packet. This keeps steady progress through the window of lost packets.

sections.title: Optional Variants and Heuristics
sections.content:
The RFC describes two variants for handling retransmit timers after partial ACKs. The Impatient variant (recommended and specified in section 3) resets the retransmit timer only after the first partial ACK. If many packets are lost, the timer may expire before all are recovered, triggering Slow-Start. The Slow-but-Steady variant resets the timer after every partial ACK, meaning the sender retransmits at most one packet per round-trip time, which is more conservative but also slower for highly lossy windows.

The RFC also defines two heuristics (optional enhancements) to invoke Fast Retransmit even when the ACK doesn't cover 'recover'. The ACK heuristic checks if the cumulative ACK jumped by at most 4 SMSS bytes, which would indicate a lost packet rather than unnecessary retransmission. The timestamp heuristic (requires TCP timestamps) uses the echoed timestamp to distinguish between a dropped retransmission and unnecessary retransmission of packets already received.
sections.plainLanguage: There are different ways to tune NewReno: you can retry fast (Impatient, which is recommended) or slow but steady. There are also optional tricks using extra information in the headers to avoid false alarms about lost packets.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
For data receivers, the RFC emphasizes sending immediate acknowledgments for out-of-order segments, even when they fill a hole. Some receivers delay ACKs waiting for the delayed ACK timer to expire, which severely limits NewReno's effectiveness by delaying the partial ACK. Implementations should acknowledge immediately.

For data senders, the RFC highlights several pitfalls: (1) avoid bursts of data when leaving Fast Recovery by limiting packets per ACK; (2) use a separate state flag to track whether Fast Recovery is active, not the duplicate ACK counter; (3) keep the 'recover' variable pulled along with the send sequence number to avoid sequence space wraparound issues; (4) correctly ignore duplicate ACKs when not in Fast Recovery to avoid spurious timeouts.
sections.plainLanguage: Receivers should reply immediately when they get out-of-order packets. Senders should be careful to avoid suddenly blasting too much data when recovery ends, and should track the recovery state properly so they don't accidentally re-enter recovery incorrectly.

sections.title: Status and Comparison with Reno
sections.content:
RFC 3782 advances NewReno's algorithms to Standards Track status, making them the recommended approach for TCP implementations that do not support SACK. The document obsoletes RFC 2582 (Experimental) and is itself obsoleted by RFC 6582. NewReno is now widely deployed in real-world TCP stacks, particularly for browsers and servers that don't support SACK.

Compared to Reno, NewReno performs significantly better with multiple packet losses and remains superior to Reno except in rare scenarios with heavy packet reordering. However, SACK (RFC 2018) remains the preferred solution when available, as it has excellent performance in both multiple-loss and reordering scenarios. NewReno is the pragmatic choice for SACK-less networks, balancing complexity and performance.
sections.plainLanguage: NewReno is now the standard way TCP should handle multiple lost packets when SACK isn't available. It does much better than Reno except when packets arrive out of order (in which case SACK is still better). SACK is the preferred choice if both ends support it.
